title: A lô? — phone calls, messages and review
title_target: A lô, em nghe đây ạ.
goal: Make phone calls and write short messages in Vietnamese — then see the whole module side by side on a single page.

writing short messages and natural well-wishes

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Cuộc gọi cuối cùng
dialogs.intro: Budi's last evening in Hà Nội before going home for the holidays. He calls Linh to invite her to a farewell dinner. Almost everything you've learned since unit 1 is in these eleven lines.

notes: **Em nghe đây is the standard way to answer the phone** — literally "I'm listening here". It's more than "hello": it tells the caller you're ready to listen. Its cousins are *Tôi nghe.* and *Vâng, tôi đây.* ("yes, it's me").
**Budi đây means "it's Budi"** — the word *đây* (here) is used to identify yourself on the phone, like English "Budi here". To ask who's calling: *Ai đấy ạ?* or *Ai gọi đấy ạ?*

**Có chuyện gì thế? means "what's up?"** and it's not a suspicious question — it's a natural, warm one when someone calls out of the blue. The reassuring answer is *Không có gì đâu, em chỉ muốn hỏi thăm thôi.* ("nothing, I just wanted to say hi").

**Notice that Budi uses *rồi* for something that hasn't happened yet**: *Thứ bảy này em về Indonesia **rồi**.* This is a typical use of *rồi*: not "I've already gone home", but "it's already time to go home, only days left". It feels like "I'm off home this Saturday, you know".

**Cảm ơn … vì … is the pattern for thanking someone for something**: *Em cảm ơn chị vì đã giúp em.* ("thank you for helping me"). ⚠️ Here *đã* really is used, because no other time word shows that the help has already happened — exactly the rule from unit 16.
**Không có gì đâu is the standard reply to thanks**, literally "it's nothing at all". Compare English "not at all" and "you're welcome". The short form is *Không có gì.*, the warmest *Có gì đâu!*

grammars.title: Making phone calls
body: Phone conversations have their own set phrases, and since there's no face to read, these phrases matter even more than face to face.

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
Meaning
rows: Cho em gặp chị Linh ạ.
Cho em gặp chị Ling ạ.
Chị Linh có nhà không ạ?
Chị Ling kó nyà không ạ?
Anh nói to hơn được không ạ?
Ang nói to hơn dượk không ạ?
Lát nữa em gọi lại nhé.
Lát nữa em gọi lại nyé.

after: ⚠️ *Nghe* means "listen" **and** "answer the phone": *Sao em không nghe máy?* = "why didn't you pick up?". *Máy* means machine, so *nghe máy* is literally "listen to the machine".
*Gọi lại* means "call back" — *lại* after a verb means "back, again", a pattern you saw in unit 11 (*quay lại*, *dừng lại*). The same little word, working in a different place.

grammars.title: Twenty units in one table
body: If a row makes you hesitate, go back to that unit and reread the dialogue aloud. Ten minutes is enough to review one unit.

head: Unit
What you've mastered
Key example
rows: possession with *của*; *đã / đang / sẽ / rồi / chưa*
*Bớt cho em một chút được không?*

after: ⚠️ **The three things most often still shaky at the end of A1**, in order of frequency: (1) tones — especially *hỏi* versus *ngã* and *huyền* versus *nặng*; (2) reading **d** as *z* and only **đ** as *d*; (3) choosing a pronoun quickly without stopping to think.
All three can only be fixed by **listening and speaking**, not by rereading. The closing pages at the back of this module give you three next steps.

blocks.text: Vietnamese messages are short, with almost no long greetings, and nearly always end with a little word from unit 17. Only one thing is a must: the right pronoun.

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
English
rows: Chị ơi, em Budi đây ạ.
Chị ơi, em Budi dây ạ.
Chị đợi em một chút nhé.
Chị dợi em một chút nyé.
Em cảm ơn chị nhiều ạ.
Em kảm ơn chị nyiều ạ.
Chúc chị cuối tuần vui vẻ!
Chúk chị kuối tuần vui vẻ!
Em xin lỗi, em quên mất ạ.
Em sin lỗi, em kwên mất ạ.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Vietnamese people write messages **without tone marks** far less often than you'd expect — tones are too important to drop. If you write *toi khong biet* without marks, the message can still be guessed but reads like a foreigner's writing. Learn to type with tone marks from the start; a Vietnamese keyboard is available on every phone.

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
English
rows: Cảm ơn chị vì tất cả ạ.
Kảm ơn chị vì tất kả ạ.
Khi nào chị sang Indonesia nhé!
Khi nào chị sang Indonesia nyé!
Chúc anh mọi điều tốt lành.
Chúk ang mọi diều tốt làng.

blocks.title: Nhớ — one word for remembering and missing
items: *Nhớ* means "remember" **and** "miss", and Vietnamese doesn't separate them at all: *Em nhớ chị.* can mean "I remember you" or "I miss you", and in practice it's almost always the second.
It's a beautiful, very characteristic merger: to miss someone is to keep remembering them. If you take home only one word from this module, this one deserves to be a candidate.

blocks.text: And one last sentence Vietnamese people say most often to a foreigner who manages to talk with them: *Tiếng Việt của em giỏi lắm!* It's almost always too much praise — and almost always sincere. Accept it with *Chị quá khen ạ.* ("you're too kind") or simply with a smile and *Cảm ơn chị ạ.*
